title: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String
summary: Return the index of the first occurrence of needle in haystack, or -1.
statement:
Return the index of the first place where `needle` occurs as a substring of `haystack`, or `-1` if it does not occur at all.

Try to write the search yourself instead of calling `indexOf`.

A simple check at every start position is O(n·m). KMP or a rolling hash brings it down to O(n + m).
constraints: Both strings have only lowercase English letters
hints: The simple approach tries every start position and compares character by character: O(n · m).
KMP avoids re-reading text: precompute for the needle the length of the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix, for every prefix.
When a mismatch happens, fall back in the needle using that table instead of moving the text pointer back. That is O(n + m).
explain: "sad" occurs at index 0 and again at index 6. The first occurrence is at index 0, so the answer is 0.

title: Rotate String
summary: Return whether s can become goal by repeatedly moving its first character to the end.
statement:
A shift moves the first character of `s` to the end, so `"abcde"` becomes `"bcdea"`. Return `true` if `s` can become `goal` after some number of shifts (including zero).

A neat test: `goal` is a rotation of `s` exactly when the two have the same length and `goal` appears inside `s + s`.
constraints: Both strings have only lowercase English letters
hints: Write s twice in a row. Every rotation of s appears inside that doubled string.
So goal is a rotation of s exactly when the lengths are equal and goal is a substring of s + s.
The length check matters: "a" is a substring of "aaaa" but not a rotation of "aa".
explain: Two shifts turn "abcde" into "bcdea" and then "cdeab", which is `goal`. So the answer is `true`.

title: Repeated Substring Pattern
summary: Return whether s can be built by repeating one of its substrings two or more times.
statement:
Return `true` if `s` can be built by taking one of its substrings and repeating it two or more times, as `"abab"` = `"ab"` + `"ab"`.

For contrast, `"aba"` cannot be built this way, and neither can `"abcabcab"`, because no piece repeats a whole number of times to fill it exactly.
hints: The repeated block must be a prefix of s, and its length must divide s.length.
Try each divisor length d < n and check whether s equals its first d characters repeated.
A neat trick: s is made of a repeated block exactly when s appears in (s + s) with the first and last characters removed. The KMP prefix table gives an O(n) check too.
explain: "abab" is "ab" written twice, so the answer is `true`.

title: Repeated String Match
summary: Return the fewest times a must be repeated so that b is a substring of the result, or -1 if impossible.
statement:
Return the minimum number of times you must repeat string `a` so that `b` becomes a substring of the result. If no number of repetitions works, return `-1`.

Repeating `"abc"` 0 times gives `""`, once gives `"abc"`, and twice gives `"abcabc"`.
constraints: Both strings have only lowercase English letters
hints: Any match of b must start inside the first copy of a.
So you need at least ceil(b.length / a.length) copies, and never more than one extra copy beyond that.
Build the repeated string with q copies and check for b; if that fails, try q + 1; otherwise the answer is −1. Rabin–Karp or KMP make the search linear.
explain: Two copies "abcdabcd" do not contain "cdabcdab", but three copies "abcdabcdabcd" do (starting at index 2). So the answer is 3.

title: Repeated DNA Sequences
summary: Return every 10-letter substring that occurs more than once in the DNA string, in any order.
statement:
A DNA sequence is a string of the letters `A`, `C`, `G` and `T`. Return every 10-letter-long substring that occurs more than once in `s`.

Return each such substring once, in any order.

Slide a 10-letter window along `s` and remember the windows you have already seen; a window seen a second time is part of the answer.
constraints: `s` has only the letters A, C, G and T
hints: Slide a window of length 10 and count the substrings you have seen.
A HashSet of seen substrings plus a set of repeated ones is simple and fast enough.
To save memory, encode each letter as 2 bits: a window is a 20-bit integer you can update in O(1) with a shift, an OR and a mask (a rolling hash).
explain: "AAAAACCCCC" appears at index 0 and again at index 10, and "CCCCCAAAAA" appears at index 5 and index 15. No other 10-letter piece repeats, so the answer is `["AAAAACCCCC","CCCCCAAAAA"]`.

title: Longest Happy Prefix
summary: Return the longest non-empty proper prefix of s that is also a suffix (overlaps allowed), or "".
statement:
A happy prefix is a non-empty prefix of `s` that is also a suffix of `s`, not counting `s` itself. The prefix and the suffix may overlap.

Return the longest happy prefix, or `""` if there is none.

This is exactly the last value of the KMP failure (prefix) function for `s`, so it can be found in linear time.
hints: Checking every length with a string comparison is O(n²).
This is exactly what the KMP prefix function computes: the length of the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix.
Build the prefix table for the whole string; the answer is s.substring(0, table[n − 1]). A rolling hash comparing prefix and suffix hashes also works.
explain: "l" is both the first and the last letter. Longer prefixes ("le", "lev", "leve") do not match the suffixes of the same length ("el", "vel", "evel"), so the answer is "l".

title: Shortest Palindrome
summary: Add the fewest characters in front of s to make it a palindrome, and return that palindrome.
statement:
You may add characters only in front of `s`. Return the shortest palindrome you can make this way.

For example "abcd" has only "a" as a palindromic start, so the answer there is "dcbabcd". Finding the longest palindromic prefix quickly is the heart of the problem.
hints: Find the longest prefix of s that is already a palindrome. Only the rest needs to be mirrored in front.
The longest palindromic prefix is the longest prefix of s that equals a suffix of reverse(s).
Run the KMP prefix function on s + "#" + reverse(s). The last value is that length L; the answer is reverse(s.substring(L)) + s.
explain: The longest palindrome at the start of "aacecaaa" is "aacecaa". Only the final "a" is left over, so putting one "a" in front gives "aaacecaaa".

title: Longest Duplicate Substring
summary: Return any longest substring that occurs at least twice in s (occurrences may overlap), or "" if none.
statement:
Return any longest substring of `s` that occurs at least twice (the occurrences may overlap). If no substring repeats, return `""`.

If several repeated substrings have the maximum length, any of them is accepted.
hints: If some substring of length L repeats, a substring of every shorter length repeats too. Binary-search the length.
To test a length L, slide a window over s with a rolling hash (Rabin–Karp) and look for a repeated hash.
Hash collisions can happen: confirm a match by comparing the actual substrings, or use two independent hashes. A suffix array also solves it.
explain: "ana" appears at index 1 and again at index 3 (the two copies overlap). No substring of length 4 appears twice, so the answer is "ana".
